In order ot reproduce it need to do following:

  1. Copy benchmark-offheap.properties file into modules/yardstick/config directory.
  2. Build yardstick mvn -B clean package -Prelease,benchmarks -DskipTests -pl modules/yardstick -am
  3. Run benchmark ./bin/benchmark-drivers-start.sh config/benchmark-offheap.properties (do it from yardstick module directory)

The problem isn't related with JIT (reproduces with -Xint option).

Also see attached logs and core dump.
item.summary: JVM crashes on Solaris (SPARC V9 arch) with SIGBUS (0xa) on frame [libjvm.so+0xc7c438] Unsafe_SetInt+0x14c

status.description: The issue is considered finished, the resolution is correct. Issues which are not closed can be reopened.

comments.comment:
All examples were ran with different marshallers and work correctly.

Yardstick benchmarks don't work with offheap caches. Driver node fails (see ticket description).

Yardstick benchmarks don't work with onheap caches in case of BinaryMarshaller and OptimizedMarshaller. Server node fails. The same problem on frame [libjvm.so+0xc7c438] Unsafe_SetInt+0x14c happens but in exchange-worker thread. Error logs don't contain stacktrace for this cases. In case of JdkMarshaller this problem doesn't happen.

Probably we also have potential problems in the following parts of Ignite (based on Unsafe.putInt() usages):

  • Optimized marshaller
  • Binary marshaller
  • Direct message writer
  • Offheap caches
  • Ignite Hadoop (shuffle message)

Looks like this is the answer: https://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-8041707
64-bit Solaris has very strict alignment rules.

Another bug which urges us to abstract-out all Unsafe usages ASAP.

In order to solve aligment problems we should use by bytes reading and writing of int's, long's, etc. in case of aligned architectures. DirectByteBuffer uses this way (see usage of unaligned flag). It looks like this (code modified sake of bravity):

    private ByteBuffer putInt(long a, int x) {
        if (unaligned) {
            unsafe.putInt(a, x);
        } else {
            Bits.putInt(a, x, bigEndian); // writes Int by bytes
        }
        return this;
    }

I created simple and dirty UnsafeWrapper class upon Unsafe that use JVM option as unaligned flag and invokes by byte methods version if this flag equals false. Tests and benchmarks work on Solaris.

So we can implement our GridUnsafe class as Unsafe wrapper that will choose method of multibyte types writing/reading using os.arch system property.
Andrey, If this is quick fix, then I think it is worthwhile to do it. I like the idea of wrapping the Unsafe methods into our GridUnsafe class and fixing the alignment issues.

Fixed: https://github.com/apache/ignite/pull/362

Waiting for TC and benchmarks results.

This PR also should fix https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/IGNITE-1493 issue.

Andrey,

I still see suspicious unsafe usages in following places:

  • GridCacheOffheapSwapEntry
  • IgniteUtils.readVersion(long ptr, boolean verEx)
  • PlatformMemoryUtils
  • PlatformOutputStreamImpl/PlatformInputStreamImpl
  • PortableOffheapInputStream/PortableOffheapOutputStream
  • BinaryObjectOffheapImpl

Are you sure 'it is safe to not use 'aligned' get/put in these places.

Please also fix javadoc warnings in GridUnsafe: 'return' is missed in many places.
I can answer for "Platforms" - definitely not safe. Changes must be applied there as well.

It requires some clarification.

Unsafe contains two group of methods: the first for memory access by address pointer and the second one for memroy access by object field offset.

For the first group methods GridUnsafe wrappers always take in account information about aligment. For the second group of methods there are two different cases of memory access^

#. Access to the object field by offset always aligned, so we can always use one int, long, etc. operation insted of ByByte-version.
#. Exception form the previous case is read/write operation upon byte arrays. This operations should be aligment aware. For this cases added Aligned methods family.

May be I use not the best naming this methos. So you are welcome with any ideas about it.

See my reply to Vladimnir below.

Javadoc fixed. PR updated.

I see several problems with this implementation.
1) Big endianees are handled incorrectly.

2) Some suspicious places in PR. E.g.

  • PlatformMemoryUtils,
  • "puts" in PortableOffheapOutputStream,
    etc.

These errors are very subtle and hard to find until another crash is reported by user. Can we get rid of paired "aligned"/"not aligned" methods and always use aligned variants? Something like this:

void putShort(@Nullable Object obj, long offset, short val) {
    if (ALIGNED) {
        if (LITTLE_ENDIAN) {
            UNSAFE.putByte(obj, offset, val & 0xFF);
            UNSAFE.putByte(obj, offset + 1, (val >> 8) & 0xFF);
        }
        else {
            UNSAFE.putByte(obj, offset, (val >> 8) & 0xFF);
            UNSAFE.putByte(obj, offset + 1, val & 0xFF);
        }
    }
    else
        UNSAFE.putShort(obj, offset, val);
}

With this approach there will be no way to make any mistake.

3) "Volatile" access are not protected with the same logic.

1) All methods of GridUnsafe use bigendian byte order. Client code is reposonsible for correct endianness handling.

2) Of course, we can always uses aligned aware methods. But why we need do it in cases where we sure that pointer/offset already aligned?

3) I can be wrong but volatile access always requires aligned access.

1) Need use native byte order in GridUnsafe

2) Current implementation is ok. But should be used carefully.

3) Need use alignment memory access in order to avoid failures.
PR updated.
Andrey, have you had a chance to test the Off-Heap functionality?

Problem places in code looks like (comments added by me):

mem.casLong(ptr + 12, qAddr, 0); // need align to 8 byte scale statically

And worst (comments added by me):

// HEADER should be aligned by 8 byte scale statically
private static final int HEADER = 4 /*hash*/ + 4 /*key-size*/  + 4 /*value-size*/ + 8 /*queue-address*/ + 8 /*next-address*/;

new IgniteBiTuple<>(addr + HEADER + keyLen, valLen); // keyLen should be aligned to 8 bytes scale at runtime.

I think that problem should be fixed as part of a separate issue because proposed fix solves problems with marshallers and allows use Ignite on Solaris and HP-UX without offheap.

Thoughts?

I have a quick fix for testing purposes and it works (all fields aligned to 8 bytes): https://github.com/agura/incubator-ignite/pull/1

But because GridUnsafeMap uses casLong method only for one field we can just change fields order like this:

private static final int HEADER = 8 /*queue-address*/ + 8 /*next-address*/ + 4 /*hash*/ + 4 /*key-size*/  + 4 /*value-size*/;

Such header requres less memory than the following:

private static final int HEADER = 8 /*hash*/ + 8 /*key-size*/  + 8 /*value-size*/ + 8 /*queue-address*/ + 8 /*next-address*/;

Andrey, to be honest I believe that off-heap should be fixed as part of this ticket as well. The whole ticket is about being able to use Ignite on Solaris platforms, and off-heap is the integral part of Ignite architecture.
Andrey, would be great if you can get a committer (Semyon?) to review the pull request for you and OK the change.

GridUnsafeDataInput and GridUnsafeDataOutput classes should use the same byte order regardles system byte order. Otherwise situations are possible when read data types will differ from written data type (it is case why OptimizedObjectStreamSelfTest.testIncorrectExternalizable fails). After fixing of byte order the rest of tests passed.

Also I think that any streams should have fixed byte order. Otherwise heterogeneous claster isn't possible. So, from my point of view, DirectByteBufferStreamImplV1 and DirectByteBufferStreamImplV2 should also have fixed byte order.

One more test is still fails on Solaris: CacheAffinityCallSelfTest.testAffinityCallRestartNode. And for now I have no idea why it happens.

Also I run full API test suite and will have results tomorrow.

See PR https://github.com/apache/ignite/pull/362

DirectByteBufferStreamImplV1 and DirectByteBufferStreamImplV2 classes modified in order to always have fixed byte order.

CacheAffinityCallSelfTest.testAffinityCallRestartNode test is incorrect and should be rewritten. The problem is in the following code snippet:

    while (!fut.isDone())
        grid(1).compute().affinityCall(CACHE_NAME, key, new CheckCallable(key, topVer, topVer + 1));

This cycle can execute too many affinityCall invokes until future completed. It leads to "Job failover failed because number of maximum failover attempts for affinity call" warning.

Many tests in Ignite Binary Objects Basic plan failed on TC. The following problems found and fixed:

  1. BinaryAbstractOutputStream.readXxxArray where Xxx is multibyte type. Incorrect positioning in case of big endian byte order.
  2. BinaryObjectOffheapImpl uses system byte order while objects always serialized with little endian byte order.
  3. BinaryObjectBuilderSelfTest and BinaryObjectBuilderNonCompactSelfTest uses system byte order while objects always serialized with little endian byte order.

Andrey,

DirectByteBufferStreamImplV1 is an old version of the protocol which is left for compatibility only. Are you sure it needs to be changed? Also, is changing DirectByteBufferStreamImplV2 is OK from compatibility standpoint? Shouldn't we introduce new protocol version for these changes?

Valentin,

You are right that compatibility will be broken. I don't think that somebody will have problems with it. But it is simple enough to introduce V3 protocol with little endian byte order in messages.
Byte order related operations reverted in DirectByteBufferStreamImplV1 and DirectByteBufferStreamImplV2 classes. New DirectByteBufferStreamImplV3 protocol implementation added.

All problems found during test execution on Solaris SPARC are fixed. Waiting for TC results.

Also I create new PR where code rebased on top of master branch: https://github.com/apache/ignite/pull/404
TC looks good. Please, review.

Started do review, have some comments so far:

Guys,

I have only one comment here, which I already expressed before - I do not like any mention of "endian" inside GridUnsafe. This just appears fundamentally wrong for me.

Java's sun.misc.Unsafe doesn't operate on endians anyhow. It just write bytes to memory. And our initial problem was alignment, not endians. If i am to do that ticket from scratch, I would only add "ALIGNMENT" flag to GridUnsafe. And all endian-related logic would reside in concrete users of GridUnsafe. This would give clear separation of concerns:
1) GridUnsafe operate on memory taking in count alignment;
2) Users of GridUnsafe decides how to deal with endians depending on their requirements.

With current implementation GridUnsafe looks virtually unusable for me. Should I need to use it, I simply would not understand which method to use in which situation.

Nevertheless, I haven't follow this ticket closely and my concern is somewhat a matter of taste. I do not ask anyone to follow it, this is just my thought.

The rest looks fine for me.

There are two use cases:

  1. Work with multibyte types in offheap memory: use GridUnsafe methods with out byte order in signature.
  2. Marshalling requires fixed byte order. Use methods that operates with byte order.

It is simple enough.
